PLOS Biology.title: PhagoCyt enables isolation of Salmonella-containing phagosomes and mapping of host and bacteria remodelling of the intracellular niche
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Ritika Chatterjee, José Luis Marin-Rubio, Francesca Romana Cianfanelli, Andrew Michael Frey, Benjamin Bernard Armando Raymond, Abeer Dannoura, Camila Valenzuela, Meihan Meng, Tiaan Heunis, Mengchun Li, Frances Sidgwick, Jost Enninga, Andrew Filby, Matthias Trost Macrophages engulf pathogens into dynamic phagosomes, which many bacteria manipulate for survival. However, isolating pure pathogen-containing phagosomes remains challenging. Here, we developed a novel flow cytometry-based isolation and ultrasensitive proteomics approach to analyse phagosomal and bacterial proteomes from macrophages infected with wild-type (WT) Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STM) or a ΔphoP mutant at 30 min and 4 hours post-infection. Our approach provides higher throughput, requires lower cell numbers and quantifies more proteins than previous techniques. Our data reveals key host-pathogen interactions, showing induction of PhoP-dependent virulence factors and novel putative proteins that shape STM’s intracellular niche. Moreover, our data indicates that bacteria-containing phagosomes recruit mitochondrial membrane for production of reactive oxygen species. These findings provide new insights into Salmonella’s manipulation of phagosomal maturation and intracellular niche formation.

PLOS Biology.title: Vertebrate paired fins are specified by an ancient dorso-ventral patterning system
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Rebecca E. Dale, Silke Berger, Sara Alaei, Marcus C. Davis, Frank J. Tulenko, Peter D. Currie The origin of paired fins was a major event in early vertebrate history that fueled the adaptive radiation of the gnathostome clade. Evidence for the conservation of ancient regulatory systems between paired and median fins supports a model in which appendage-patterning mechanisms first evolved in the midline and were later redeployed to a new embryonic context, the flank. However, while paired fins and limbs are asymmetric along the dorsoventral (DV) axis, the equivalent axis does not exist in median fins, which are symmetric across the midline, raising questions of how DV patterning evolved. Here, we combine genetic tools in zebrafish with comparative expression analyses in representative ray-finned and cartilaginous fishes to show that a subset of limb DV patterning genes are expressed during median fin development. Using genetic lineage tracing of the canonical limb dorsalizing factor lmx1bb, we further demonstrate that, although lmx1bb-derived cells occupy distinct spatial domains across fin types, a subset of this lineage is fated to differentiate into fin ray osteoblasts in both paired and median fins. To test the potential conservation of regulatory modules across fin types, we generated a series of deletion mutants for two known lmx1b mouse limb enhancers, LARM1 and LARM2, that we show are partially conserved upstream of zebrafish lmx1bb. These experiments revealed that LARM function is essential for dorsoventral patterning of the paired pectoral and pelvic fins of zebrafish but is dispensable for formation of the unpaired dorsal and anal fins. Collectively, these data support the conservation of an ancient LARM-Lmx1b dorsal determination system in the paired fins of osteichthyans, challenge models proposing simple co-option of a pre-existing median fin gene regulatory network and suggest that the acquisition of this regulatory module may have been a key early step in the evolution of the paired fin DV patterning axis.

Genome Research.title: Ultrafast alignment-free detection of viral genome variation with bronko.
Genome Research.abstract: As viral sequencing datasets continue to grow, traditional alignment-based variant calling pipelines are becoming computationally prohibitive. To address these challenges, we developed bronko, an ultrafast alignment-free framework for detecting viral variation directly from sequencing data. The novel computational approach implemented in bronko allows scaling to massive viral sequencing datasets and has four key components: i) a locality-sensitive bucketing function to rapidly identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) relative to reference(s), ii) a direct k-mer count pseudo-mapping approach that approximates a pileup without alignment, iii) a greedy de novo assembly algorithm to reconstruct mutation-dense regions and indels and iv) a streaming-based sliding window outlier test to estimate baseline noise across the genome and precisely differentiate real minor variants from noise. Together, these components yield near-linear computational complexity with respect to sequencing depth, enabling bronko to process thousands of viral samples rapidly on modest hardware. Our results are threefold: 1) On simulated amplicon sequencing, bronko recovers variants with higher precision and comparable recall to existing tools while running up to one to three orders of magnitude faster; 2) bronko generates sequence alignments directly from sequencing data, with SNP content nearly identical to that of whole-genome alignment while also running in a fraction of the time, and 3) applying bronko to longitudinal sequencing data from chronically infected SARS-CoV-2 patients revealed consistent patterns of intrahost diversification and adaptive mutations over time. Altogether, these results demonstrate bronko's potential as a scalable tool for large-scale viral genomic analyses, overcoming longstanding computational barriers for intrahost and interhost characterization of viral variation.

Genome Research.title: Derivation of doxorubicin mutational signatures in cancer.
Genome Research.abstract: Doxorubicin is a chemotherapeutic agent used for the treatment of solid and hematopoietic malignancies. Doxorubicin acts as a DNA intercalator and inhibits the topoisomerase II enzyme, leading to double-stranded breaks. We hypothesize that doxorubicin mutagenesis leads to a nonrandom pattern of somatic mutations on the genome, termed a mutational signature. We expose cells to doxorubicin using two different methodologies: (1) continuous exposure of a constant dose of doxorubicin and whole-genome sequencing of single-cell clones (previously published methodology) and (2) pulsed exposure of escalating doses of doxorubicin and whole-genome sequencing of a bulk population. We first confirm that the methodologies do not yield differing results through previously published cisplatin-exposed single-cell clone genome data compared with the dose escalation and bulk genome data. We then derive two doxorubicin signatures. The first, SBS-doxorubicin-1, is defined by an abundance of C > A mutations. The second, SBS-doxorubicin-2, is defined by a higher occurrence of T > C mutations. We then assess for the presence of our signatures within the genomes of patients treated with a doxorubicin-containing regimen. Across 10 bulk immune sorted samples from three patients with follicular lymphoma/diffuse large B cell lymphoma, as well as two metastatic samples from one patient with renal medullary carcinoma, we are able to detect both signatures in 83% of samples, with remaining samples harboring either signature. In summary, we experimentally derive two doxorubicin mutational signatures and demonstrate their presence in patient samples.

Genome Biology and Evolution.title: Conserved and taxon-restricted orthogroup expansions of pan-eukaryotic protein complexes.
Genome Biology and Evolution.abstract: Protein complexes are central to cell biology and typically verified via a combination of interaction data, complete genome sequencing and comprehensive protein-coding gene predictions for reference eukaryotes. However, this information is lacking for non-reference eukaryotes. Protein complexes can be predicted in species for which no interaction data is available by mapping orthology of verified protein complex components from reference eukaryotes to predicted proteomes. Studies that map conservation of protein complex components by orthology are often limited to a small number of protein queries, an under-representation of non-reference, microbial eukaryotes and are scattered across the literature. Here, I integrate orthology and protein interaction data by mapping proteins of experimentally verified complexes to orthogroups of proteins spanning 31 diverse eukaryotes. Proteins within complex-harbouring orthogroups are retained and distributed more evenly across taxa than non-complex orthogroups. I identified 184 universal orthogroups that included orthologs of known protein complex components from all 31 eukaryotes, consistent with a conserved core repertoire, likely present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA). I generated the protein complex orthology cartographer (PCOC) suite to find significant duplications and reductions of proteins in universal orthogroups across and between eukaryotes. This revealed both multi-copy and notably single-copy proteins, in all queried species, from the exosome, spliceosome, proteasome, small-ribosomal processome, tRNA synthetases, MCM complexes and RNA polymerase III. Case analyses of Naegleria gruberi and Guillardia theta highlight taxon-specific expansions and show how broader protist inclusion improves domain-wide inference of eukaryotic protein-complex evolution.

Genome Biology and Evolution.title: The evolutionary history of transporters of the plastid outer envelope of Chloroplastida- a structure-sequence comparison.
Genome Biology and Evolution.abstract: Plant metabolism heavily relies on plastids, derived from once free-living organisms. However, how two distinct organisms merged into one remains currently only partially understood. Protein-mediated metabolite exchange across the double-membrane plastid envelope is essential for plant cell function. Here, we investigate the evolutionary origins of plastid outer envelope proteins (OEPs) involved in these transport processes. The mosaic nature of the nuclear genome and the deep evolutionary distance since plastid acquisition are major challenges. To address them, we combine sequence-based analyses with emerging structure-based tools, which together enable more sensitive evolutionary comparisons than traditional methods alone. To uncover distinct evolutionary trajectories, we focused on 27 OEPs from metabolite transport and protein import, with diverse structures. We found that the β-barrel proteins involved in metabolite transport were recruited in a stepwise manner and structural homologs of some OEPs point to early recruitment via endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT). Protein import is sequence-wise conserved across Archaeplastida, although refinements occur across Chloroplastdia and structural turnover is implicated. Notably, OEP40 shows a recent structural rearrangement, lacking clear structural homologs in plants other than Arabidopsis, yet retaining sequence conservation across all major land-plant lineages. The JASSY-like family is found across plastid-bearing species, while true JASSY orthologs emerged in embryophytes likely via a stable recruitment of the characteristic lipid-binding domain. Overall, our findings highlight the dynamic nature of the plastid outer envelope and show how new functions could evolve through structural reshaping and novel domain recruitment.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Porphyromonas gingivalis TonB2 is required for protease maturation and cell surface remodeling.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] TonB-dependent transport systems are essential for nutrient acquisition in Gram-negative bacteria. Although Porphyromonas gingivalis, a major periodontal pathogen, encodes multiple TonB-dependent receptors (TBDT), the identity and function of its TonB energy transducers remain poorly understood. Here, we identified three putative TonB proteins encoded by PG0633 (TonB1), PG0785 (TonB2), and PG2185 (TonB3), and generated a TonB2-deficient strain to investigate its biological role. Bioinformatics analyses revealed that TonB2 possesses unique structural features conserved within members of the Cytophaga-Flavobacterium-Bacteroides (CFB) group while retaining a C-terminal domain homologous to well-characterized TonB proteins from Helicobacter pylori and Escherichia coli. Both protein sequence similarity and genomic organization further support the conservation of TonB2 among members of the phylum Bacteroidota. Loss of TonB2 resulted in extensive proteomic remodeling, including increased abundance of proteins involved in gene regulation, translation, protection against oxidative and nitrosative stress, and glycosylation, accompanied by decreased levels of proteins associated with polysaccharide export, efflux systems, and lipoprotein biogenesis. Phenotypic analyses demonstrated that the TonB2-deficient mutant was impaired in heme accumulation at the cell surface, exhibited reduced gingipain activity, and displayed diminished capsule production. Furthermore, although the mutant adhered to and invaded host cells more efficiently than the wild type, its intracellular survival was significantly compromised. Collectively, these findings reveal an unexpected role for TonB2 in cell surface biogenesis, virulence-associated functions, and host-pathogen interactions, expanding our understanding of TonB system versatility and suggesting functional crosstalk between the TonB and Tol energy transduction systems. [IMPORTANCE] The TonB system is a major energy-transducing complex in Gram-negative bacteria, but its functions outside classical nutrient acquisition remain poorly understood, particularly in the phylum Bacteroidota. Here, we show that Porphyromonas gingivalis TonB2 plays a role distinct from canonical TonB-dependent transport. Rather than primarily supporting iron uptake, TonB2 contributes to gingipain maturation, capsule production, cell surface organization, and interactions with host cells. These diverse phenotypes suggest a broader role in coordinating cell envelope biogenesis and integrity. We propose that TonB2 has been adapted to couple energy transduction with envelope maintenance, revealing an unexpected functional diversification of TonB proteins that supports virulence and cellular homeostasis.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Catabolite activator protein and quorum sensing cross-control group behaviors in Vibrio campbellii.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Vibrio species adapt to different niches by sensing and responding to environmental signals such as nutrients, host cues, and quorum sensing autoinducers. Vibrio campbellii uses the master quorum sensing transcription factor LuxR to control the expression of hundreds of genes at high cell density. Furthermore, many gamma-proteobacteria use the global transcription factor catabolite activator protein (CAP) to control numerous physiologically relevant pathways, many of which are also modulated by quorum sensing, such as competence, biofilm formation, and carbon metabolism. However, the extent to which these two global transcription factors overlap to co-regulate gene expression and bacterial behaviors is understudied. In this work, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled with high-throughput Illumina sequencing (ChIP-seq) and RNA-seq to determine the individual and combined regulons of CAP and LuxR in V. campbellii. We found that CAP and LuxR co-occupied 11 promoters to synergistically or antagonistically co-regulate genes involved with metabolism, respiration, and virulence. It was previously proposed that CAP and LuxR both bound the bioluminescence (luxCDABE) promoter to co-regulate these genes, and our RNA-seq data showed that these were indeed the most strongly co-regulated genes. However, our ChIP-seq data revealed that only LuxR bound the luxCDABE promoter in vivo. This pattern of co-regulation-where both CAP and LuxR strongly impact transcription, but only LuxR binds the promoter-was the most common mechanism observed. Our model for bioluminescence regulation is that CAP indirectly activates luxCDABE expression through the regulation of an intermediate factor. This study established new connections between the global gene regulatory networks underpinning nutrient sensing and population sensing. [IMPORTANCE] Vibrio bacteria (vibrios) colonize and infect diverse marine hosts, including corals, fish, oysters, and shrimp, and can also cause life-threatening human infections, all of which are rising annually due to increasing ocean temperatures. To develop effective treatments against Vibrio infections, it is critical to understand the global gene regulation mechanisms vibrios use that enable pathogenic lifestyles. Signal transduction systems in bacteria are well-characterized; however, how vibrios coordinate global gene expression changes in response to multiple environmental inputs is understudied. Here, we determined how the aquaculture pathogen Vibrio campbellii regulates global gene expression in response to bacterial population signals and nutrient availability signals. Our findings help contextualize how vibrios respond to their fluctuating environments in nature.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Bacterial adaptation is associated with tryptophan metabolism and persistence of nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Bacterial adaptation to the nutritional environment of the host is critical for infection. We hypothesize that responses to nutrient stress through microevolution enhance invasion, intracellular bacterial community (IBC) formation, and persistence of nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHI). We previously identified a mutant that arose during prolonged nutrient deprivation and exhibited in vitro persistence and increased IBC formation during experimental otitis media (OM). A single mutation in the gene encoding cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase reprioritizes NTHI metabolism during biofilm growth in this evolved strain with a significant increase in all proteins involved in tryptophan biosynthesis. Given the importance of tryptophan and tryptophan metabolites in host immunity and bacterial virulence, we evaluated the contribution of tryptophan biosynthesis and import on NTHI pathogenesis. Through mutational analyses, NTHI viability in vitro is dependent on tryptophan biosynthesis but independent of tryptophan import. We also observed decreased persistence of IBCs in the absence of tryptophan biosynthesis. In an experimental model of OM, both tryptophan biosynthesis and import mutant strains demonstrated increased fitness compared to the parental strain. The NTHI trp operon has a distinct organization from Escherichia coli and contains an ortholog of ydfG, an NADP-dependent 3-hydroxyl acid dehydrogenase, that contributes to oxidative stress resistance. This ydfG ortholog exhibits greater frequency in mucosal-associated NTHI strains, as compared with commensal or invasive strains. Understanding the underlying mechanisms that NTHI use to respond and survive within the host environment, particularly tryptophan biosynthesis, will inform the development of therapeutics to attenuate current NTHI infections and limit recurrent episodes of OM.IMPORTANCEBacteria exquisitely adapt to environmental cues to survive and, in some cases, cause disease. We observed that bacteria starved for heme-iron evolve to increase the expression of tryptophan biosynthesis genes. We determined that loss of tryptophan biosynthesis decreased intracellular bacterial survival. In an experimental model of middle ear infection, both tryptophan biosynthesis and import mutant strains demonstrated increased fitness compared to the parental strain. We determined that the organization of tryptophan biosynthesis and transport genes is distinct and contains a gene that encodes a protein that contributes to oxidative stress resistance. This gene exhibits greater frequency in mucosal-associated NTHI strains, as compared with commensal or invasive strains. These data reveal coordination of tryptophan metabolism with oxidative stress resistance for bacterial persistence.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Growth on human serum albumin drives large genomic inversion in Porphyromonas gingivalis.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Insertion sequence transposable elements can bring about breakage and rejoining of chromosomal DNA in inverted orientations. Genomic inversions are a type of chromosomal rearrangement that significantly influence gene expression, yet our understanding of what conditions and processes drive these rearrangements remains unclear. Importantly, these inversions are typically reversible and therefore dynamic. Using long reads to evaluate genome structure, this study revealed that populations of some strains of the oral anaerobe Porphyromonas gingivalis have two distinct genome arrangements, and the large 1.5 Mbp inversion resulting from these rearrangements is controlled by matching ISPg2 transposase elements. Strains that can rearrange their genomes undergo early autolysis when grown on human serum albumin (HSA) as a substrate, yet the strains lacking the matching ISPg2 elements do not. Intriguingly, a subset of cells within the population survives after lysis, and the inverted sub-population orientation becomes dominant. We propose that P. gingivalis maintains different genotypic subpopulations with varying phenotypes within its population as a bet-hedging strategy, where some of the cells will continue to persist after most of the cells lyse, thereby improving overall survival. The findings presented here provide further confirmation of striking differences between P. gingivalis strains and new insights into the impact of genome rearrangement on P. gingivalis physiology by using HSA as a biologically relevant substrate for growth. [IMPORTANCE] In bacteria, some regions of chromosomal DNA (called insertion sequence transposable elements) can exchange with each other and cause large sections of a genome to flip around in the opposite direction. This study identified a dynamic 1.5 Mbp chromosomal inversion in Porphyromonas gingivalis mediated by ISPg2 elements. Triggered by growth on human serum albumin, this rearrangement modulates autolysis while allowing a resilient subpopulation to dominate. Our findings highlight a bet-hedging strategy as a vital mechanism for P. gingivalis persistence, offering new insights into how genomic plasticity drives survival in biologically relevant growth conditions.

mSphere.title: Comparative genomics of the skin microbiome and associated isolates of patients undergoing mastectomy with immediate breast reconstruction.
mSphere.abstract: Mastectomy with immediate breast implant reconstruction (IBIR) is an increasingly common component of breast cancer treatment; however, these procedures carry a substantial risk of surgical site infections (SSIs) and noninfectious wound complications (NIWCs). We hypothesized that the local skin microbiota may contribute to the development of post-operative complications, in part by serving as a reservoir for pathobionts, such as Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes. We collected skin and intraoperative samples from 60 patients undergoing mastectomy with IBIR. To evaluate longitudinal shifts in community composition, we performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing of 151 breast and axilla skin swabs collected at pre- and post-operative time points. Using a comprehensive culture approach, we recovered diverse cultivable organisms and selected 232 S. epidermidis and 130 C. acnes isolates from skin swabs, implant swabs, and seroma fluid for whole-genome sequencing and comparative genomic analysis. We observed perturbations to community structure in the breast and axilla following mastectomy. These shifts were characterized by a significant and persistent depletion of Corynebacterium spp., which did not resolve in patients who subsequently developed an SSI. We also uncovered outcome-specific genomic signatures in S. epidermidis isolates, which may offer mechanistic insight into the role of this species in SSI and NIWC development. Importantly, we also identified genomic signatures detectable prior to mastectomy and infection diagnosis that may offer clinical utility toward predicting post-operative complications. Together, these findings illustrate the importance of the skin microbiome in SSI and NIWC development following mastectomy with IBIR.IMPORTANCEAn improved understanding of the relationship between surgical sites and adjacent resident skin microbiota can help identify which patients are at increased risk for developing surgical site infections and noninfectious wound complications. By characterizing bacterial communities before mastectomy with immediate breast reconstruction and during subsequent healing, we sought to evaluate how changes in community composition may contribute to the development of post-operative complications. We also performed in-depth genomic analyses of Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes isolates recovered from patients to identify genetic components that may determine whether an isolate protects or predisposes patients toward development of post-operative complications. Last, we identified genomic signatures detectable prior to surgery and infection diagnosis that are correlated with patient outcome, which may serve as informative biomarkers to inform patient care.

mSphere.title: An antibiotic-treated mouse model reveals the progression of intestinal botulism.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Intestinal botulism, including infant botulism and adult intestinal toxemia botulism, is a life-threatening disease caused by intestinal infection with Clostridium botulinum (Cb) spores. Infants are particularly susceptible to Cb infection because of their immature gut microbiota, whereas healthy adults are generally protected by gut microbiota-mediated colonization resistance. Thus, immature gut microbiota or gut dysbiosis is thought to permit Cb colonization. However, the mechanisms underlying colonization resistance and disease progression remain poorly characterized. Here, using adult mice with antibiotic-induced dysbiosis, we established a model for studying Cb infection and characterized intestinal colonization, bacterial expansion, botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) accumulation, and disease progression during intestinal botulism. Intestinal botulism developed in antibiotic-treated mice after intragastric administration of strain 62A spores, whereas untreated adult mice showed no symptoms. In antibiotic-treated mice, Cb expanded over time in fecal samples, followed by accumulation of serotype A BoNT (BoNT/A), which correlated with the progression of botulism symptoms. Cb growth and BoNT/A accumulation occurred mainly in the cecum and colon, but not in the small intestine. Furthermore, this mouse model was applicable to the analysis of intestinal botulism caused by other Cb strains, including 7I03-H, Okra, and Osaka05. Taken together, our findings clarify key aspects of intestinal botulism pathogenesis. This mouse model may provide a useful platform for elucidating the mechanisms underlying intestinal botulism, including infant botulism, and for developing novel therapeutic strategies. [IMPORTANCE] Botulism is a life-threatening disease caused by botulinum neurotoxin, one of the most powerful toxins known. In intestinal botulism, Clostridium botulinum spores enter the intestine, grow there, and release toxin inside the body. However, the detailed process by which intestinal botulism develops remains poorly understood. In this study, we established a mouse model that allows the progression of intestinal botulism to be examined over time. Using this model, we showed that bacterial growth in the intestine, accumulation of biologically active toxins, and worsening of symptoms are closely linked. We also identified the cecum and colon as the main sites of bacterial colonization and toxin accumulation. This model can be used to analyze multiple C. botulinum strains with different characteristics and provides a useful tool for understanding how intestinal botulism develops and for guiding future preventive and therapeutic strategies.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: RNA sequencing depth guidelines for the study of alternative splicing.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: A key parameter in the experimental design of RNA-seq projects is the choice of sequencing depth. Considering a limited budget, one needs to find a trade-off between the number of samples and the sensitivity of the analysis, particularly concerning lowly expressed genes. While previous studies have proposed a lower bound for the comprehensive analysis of differential gene expression, for the analysis of alternative splicing, it has only been proposed for human adipose tissue. However, alternative splicing differs across tissues and conditions. We analyzed publicly available and newly generated deep-sequenced paired-end RNA-seq samples (between 150 and >500 million reads, read length 50-150 bp) from human buffy coat cells and diverse sets of tissues, including gluteal subcutaneous fat, heart, and hypothalamus. Our results show that the sequencing depth typically used in published cohorts is not sufficient to comprehensively capture the landscape of alternative splicing. This motivates the use of deeper sequencing or long-read technologies in future studies. Toward this goal, we offer guidelines and a website (https://sequencing-depth4splicing.com/) for choosing a suitable sequencing depth.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: The balance between R-loops and RNAPII occupancy determines the outcome of transcription-replication conflicts.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Maintaining genome integrity requires the precise coordination of replication and transcription. While R-loops are known to cause transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs), the precise nature of the barrier, whether it is the RNA:DNA hybrid itself, the stalled RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII), or a combination of both, remains elusive. Using live-cell imaging in yeast to monitor a single R-loop prone locus in real time, we demonstrate that wild-type replisomes traverse R-loop enriched transcription units with high efficiency. We find that while R-loops initially repress transcription, replisome passage prompts a robust recovery of transcription activity. Indeed, we discover that R-loops serve a critical regulatory function by suppressing excessive RNAPII occupancy. In an RNAPII mutant with high DNA affinity, the enzymatic removal of R-loops leads to a pile-up of RNAPII molecules, creating a barrier to replication, more severe than the R-loops themselves. Thus, our findings reveal a dual nature of R-loops: while they can be obstacles and repress transcription, they can also serve as a physiological buffer that prevents the formation of high-density RNAPII 'trains'. These findings establish that the precise regulation of both R-loop levels and RNAPII density is critical for preventing harmful TRCs and maintaining genome stability.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Truncated APC regulates alternative splicing by interacting with DDX21 in colorectal cancer.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Truncating mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene-a key driver of colorectal cancer (CRC) initiation-frequently lead to the production of a truncated APC protein (Trunc-APC). However, its post-transcriptional roles and oncogenic potential remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that Trunc-APC functions as an RNA-binding protein, directly associating with pre-mRNA via its N-terminal 1-169 amino acid region to regulate widespread alternative splicing (AS) in CRC cells. Specifically, Trunc-APC promotes exon inclusion in ARHGEF11, producing an oncogenic isoform that is associated with enhanced Bcl-xL/BAX complex formation and reduced apoptosis. Mechanistically, Trunc-APC interacts with the RNA helicase DDX21 and facilitates SF3B complex recruitment to pre-mRNA, thereby modulating splicing patterns. Notably, treatment with the splicing inhibitor Madrasin significantly reduced tumor burden in ApcMin/+ CRC mice, indicating strong antitumor efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish Trunc-APC as a novel regulator of alternative splicing and a promoter of CRC progression, and highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting the Trunc-APC/DDX21/SF3B axis in CRC.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: A RARγ-SMARCA5 chromatin-remodeling axis stabilizes AR luminal programs and opposes lineage plasticity in prostate cancer.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: In prostate cancer (PCa), epigenomic mechanisms drive resistance to androgen receptor (AR) signaling inhibitors, such as enzalutamide (enza). We tested whether retinoic acid receptor gamma (RARγ) shapes the epigenome to direct AR transcription, promote luminal identity, and limit enza resistance. RARγ restoration in enza-resistant 22Rv1 cells induced a large RARγ complex containing its coactivator TACC1 and the chromatin remodeler ISWI ATPase SMARCA5. RARγ restoration expanded and redistributed the AR cistrome toward active promoters, enhancers, and unique super-enhancers and increased the overlap with H3K27ac. RARγ restoration also increased SMARCA5 promoter-proximal binding that overlapped with G2/M-enriched AR cistrome, linking AR redistribution to cell cycle-associated chromatin engagement, including at luminal genes. In 22Rv1 and LNCaP C4-2 (also enza-resistant), RARγ restoration directed the AR transcriptome toward luminal differentiation. A miR-96 antagomir (targeting RARγ) mirrored the impact of RARγ restoration. RARγ antagonized the actions of the master lineage regulator ONECUT2 at the cistrome and transcriptome level and these antagonized genes were significantly associated with alternative lineages in murine PCa models of lineage plasticity and enza responsiveness and lineage plasticity in human PCa cohorts. These findings identify RARγ as a regulator of a chromatin remodeling mechanism that sustains luminal AR programs and opposes therapeutic resistance.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Bipartite DNA-binding domain of transcription factor BCL11B binds clustered short DNA sequence motifs.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: B-cell leukemia/lymphoma 11B (BCL11B), despite its name, is a key regulator of T-cell development, lineage specification, and T-cell malignancies. BCL11B contains a bipartite DNA-binding domain composed of two C2H2 zinc finger arrays: low-affinity ZF2-3 and high-affinity ZF4-6. These arrays recognize similar six-nucleotide motifs, TG(n)CC(n), as seven of the eight DNA base-contacting residues are conserved between them. The most conserved interactions involve the central GG dinucleotides, recognized by arginine and lysine residues at the key base-interacting positions of ZF3 and ZF5. We determined eight crystal structures of ZF2-3 bound to 12- or 20-base pair DNA duplexes containing either one or two binding motifs. The structures reveal that ZF2-3 recognizes DNA with remarkable configurational flexibility, binding motifs on either the same or opposite DNA strands with variable spacing in three relative orientations: head-to-tail (or tail-to-head), head-to-head, and tail-to-tail. Analysis of BCL11B ChIP-seq peaks revealed a strong enrichment of 1-bp-spaced, same-orientation TGACC(c/t) motif pairs. We also examined six neurodevelopmental disorder-associated missense variants affecting DNA base-contacting residues. Substitutions that replace bulky, positively charged arginine or lysine with smaller or hydrophobic amino acids weaken DNA-binding affinity and specificity, whereas substitutions between asparagine and lysine alter base recognition preferences.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Strand-displacement amplification reduces structure-induced PCR bias and preserves structurally diverse aptamers during SELEX.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Stable secondary structures are important for aptamer folding and target recognition, but they can introduce structure-dependent amplification bias during Systematic Evolution of Ligands by Exponential Enrichment (SELEX), with G-quadruplexes (G4s) representing the most demanding case. Here, we introduce strand-displacement SELEX (SD-SELEX), which employs a polymerase with robust 5'→3' strand-displacement activity to improve the amplification of structured templates. Comparative analyses showed that SD polymerase efficiently amplified hairpin- and G4-forming templates, whereas Taq polymerase exhibited structure-dependent amplification variability. In parallel thrombin SELEX experiments, SD-SELEX achieved 37-fold greater structural preservation and 65-fold higher batch-to-batch reproducibility than Taq-SELEX over 11 rounds. High-throughput sequencing further showed that SD-SELEX maintained G4 motif representation and progressively enriched the known 15-mer thrombin-binding aptamer through round 8, after which it was gradually replaced by newly identified G4 variants, whereas Taq-SELEX progressively depleted these sequences. SD-SELEX also identified novel G4 aptamers with affinities comparable to that of the reference aptamer, whereas representative Taq-SELEX candidates generally showed weaker binding. A parallel selection against VEGF-165 showed the same divergence, with SD-SELEX retaining structurally complex sequences and a previously reported functional motif that were progressively lost under Taq. Thus, SD-SELEX primarily improves aptamer discovery by reducing structure-induced amplification bias and preserving structurally diverse functional candidates, rather than by substantially increasing affinity alone.

Cell-free expression and NGS-powered substrate profiling reveal a thermostable metagenomic meganuclease from an extreme environment with novel specificity.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: As an alternative to historical enzyme isolation, metagenomic databases (e.g. MGnify) provide information on vast unculturable microbial diversity, including extreme environments, and constitute an enormous source of functional proteins. Conservative mining of these data by close sequence homology alone tends to identify merely different versions of known enzymes. Here we present a discovery strategy for meganucleases based on wider capture of less homologous enzymes in metagenomic databases, and incorporating metadata with their homology. We use cell-free expression to bypass host incompatibility and the need for purification, along with deep sequencing for experimental assessment of substrate specificity and cleavage pattern, thereby circumventing classical gel-based profiling. Specifically, we discovered the temperature-stable (>55°C), intron-encoded LAGLIDADG meganuclease I-MG11 that recognizes a GC-rich 17 base pair sequence to generate 4-nt palindromic 3'-overhangs-the first monomeric meganuclease to produce such overhangs. Co-folding models of I-MG11 bound to DNA provide a structural context for enzyme-DNA interactions, highlighting differences from other monomeric LAGLIDADG meganucleases (e.g. I-SceI) shaped by InDels (insertion-deletions) in the DNA-binding region that may cause specificity changes. Our strategy streamlines general bona fide identification and annotation of meganucleases, while the unique properties of I-MG11 expand the toolbox of molecular genome engineering.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Microfluidic concatemer sequencing unveils cooperative and competitive enhancer clusters in gene regulation.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Chromatin looping plays a pivotal role in eukaryotic gene regulation; however, technical limitations have hindered the comprehensive characterization of higher-order interactions among genomic loci. As a result, key questions, such as whether enhancers function cooperatively or competitively at the single-molecule and ensemble levels, remain largely unresolved. Here, we present Drop-t, a novel microfluidics-based method that enables systematic profiling of higher-order chromatin architecture at both the single-molecule and population scales. We demonstrate that Drop-t is not only resistant to common ligation-induced DNA entanglements, which frequently cause nanopore clogging, but also provides greater relevance for elucidating regulatory mechanisms compared to existing ligation-free approaches. Using Drop-t, we uncovered extensive, previously underappreciated non-specific enhancer-promoter interactions (EPIs) and showed that these may influence transcriptional variability by competing with specific EPIs. Notably, we identified two major gene classes, dictator genes and leader genes, based on whether their promoters are predominantly regulated by competitive or cooperative specific EPIs, respectively. Together, our findings established Drop-t as a powerful tool for decoding the higher-order organizational principles of chromatin architecture and their impact on transcriptional regulation and variability.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Transcription factor 3 cooperates with CXXC finger protein 1 to regulate histone H3K4 trimethylation and developmental competence in mouse oocytes.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: During oogenesis, the establishment of oocyte-specific gene expression relies on epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling. Both histone modifications and transcription factors are crucial for the oocyte to acquire developmental competence; however, the mechanisms involved remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify transcription factor 3 (TCF3), an E-protein family member, as a key maternal regulator of oocyte developmental potential. Oocyte-specific deletion of Tcf3 results in female infertility, characterized by impaired meiotic maturation and early embryonic arrest at the two-cell stage. These defects are associated with defective maternal mRNA clearance and disrupted establishment of the H3K4me3 landscape in maturing oocytes. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that TCF3 directs H3K4me3 deposition at target gene promoters through interaction with CXXC finger protein 1 (CXXC1), the core subunit of the SETD1 histone methyltransferase complex. Importantly, this TCF3-CXXC1 interaction depends on their DNA-binding activity, highlighting the specificity of TCF3 in coordinating with CXXC1 to regulate maternal target genes, such as Pabpn1l. Together, our findings uncover a transcription factor-driven mechanism of epigenetic reprogramming that is essential for the maternal-to-zygotic transition.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Allele-selective targeting of uromodulin by antisense oligonucleotides reduces aggregates and kidney damage in a mouse model of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD) arises from gain-of-toxic-function mutations in the UMOD gene coding for uromodulin, the most abundant protein excreted in normal urine. Mutant uromodulin accumulates in the cells lining the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle, leading to intracellular aggregates, cellular stress, and kidney damage. Here, we demonstrate that an antisense gapmer oligonucleotide (ASO) designed against the representative c.553C > A (p.R185S) UMOD mutation produced allele-selective silencing of the mutant messenger RNA and protein in kidney cells. Short-term administration of a murine ASO analogue in the established Umod  R186S/+ mouse model of ADTKD suppressed uromodulin and lowered tubular damage, whereas a non-targeting scrambled control was inactive. After a 4-week treatment, ASO accumulation in the Umod  R186S/+ kidneys reached ∼320 000 copies per TAL cell, quantified using a sensitive splint-ligation assay. The ASO treatment suppressed premature mutant uromodulin and its toxic aggregates in Umod  R186S/+ kidneys, whereas it had no effects on wild-type uromodulin in Umod  +/+ kidneys. Notably, the ASO improved tubular function and decreased kidney tubulointerstitial inflammation in Umod  R186S/+ mice. This work offers a roadmap for antisense therapy to treat ADTKD-UMOD and substantiates the therapeutic potential of ASOs in disorders of the kidney tubule.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Archaeal histones coordinate conserved DNA sequence motifs to promote CRISPR adaptive immunity.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Archaea and bacteria acquire resistance to viruses by integrating fragments of foreign DNA at the beginning of a CRISPR locus. In the archaeon Pyrococcus furiosus, histones bind the leader to promote specific integration at the first CRISPR repeat. However, it remains unknown whether archaeal CRISPR leaders contain conserved DNA sequence motifs required for integration. Here, we analyze 542 archaeal CRISPR leaders found across Thermococcales and Methanococcales. We identify 36 motifs found up to 500 bps upstream of archaeal CRISPR loci. Scrambling or truncating novel motifs or histone binding sites found 100-400 bps upstream of the P. furiosus CRISPR modestly decreases integration efficiency. However, mutation of motif T2, which overlaps with the proximal histone site and is adjacent to the CRISPR, ablates both histone-mediated and histone-independent integration. Mutations tiled across T2 reveal that a pyrimidine at position -3 of the leader is required for histone-independent integration, and basepairs -4 to -19 are required for histone-mediated integration. T2 is found in most Thermococcales, and a similar sequence is found in most Methanococcales leaders, suggesting this motif may be a broadly conserved element that facilitates CRISPR adaptive immunity across taxonomic orders. These data shed light on the sequence requirements for histone-mediated DNA integration.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: The anti-phage defense system GAPS4 is a double-edged sword that sensitizes bacteria to DNA-damaging agents.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The arms race between bacteria and bacteriophages (phages) gave rise to multiple layers of antagonistic mechanisms, many of which remain unexplored. Here, we investigated the widespread anti-phage defense system GAPS4. We found that GAPS4 forms a heterotetrameric complex containing active PD-(D/E)xK phosphodiesterase domains. It is triggered upon sensing DNA damage, leading to genomic DNA degradation and cell suicide. We further demonstrated that this activation mechanism renders GAPS4 a double-edged sword, sensitizing bacteria to various DNA-targeting antibacterial agents. Collectively, our findings reveal a possible evolutionary trade-off between anti-phage defense and immunity against interbacterial antagonism.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: iCellOmics: connecting multi-omics profiles and phenotype evidence across industrially relevant cell lines.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Industrially relevant cell lines include direct production hosts for biologics, vaccines, and viral vectors, as well as biomedical models that serve as references for host-cell engineering and comparative studies. However, their genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic profiles, together with literature-derived phenotype information, remain distributed across different repositories, project outputs, and publications. Here, we present iCellOmics (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/icellomics), an open-access database that integrates multi-omics data for industrially relevant cell lines within a unified data and analysis framework. The current release covers 17 cell lines and provides reference genomes for seven species, encompassing 144 018 protein-coding genes, 170 408 888 genomic variants, 673 differential-expression comparisons, 30 distinct single-cell RNA-seq BioProjects comprising 1 047 274 cells, 287 089 415 ATAC-seq peaks, 37 213 deduplicated literature-curated gene-phenotype relationships spanning 104 standardized phenotype subcategories. The database supports both cell line-centric browsing of available datasets and gene-centric exploration of cross-omics analysis results. Additionally, iCellOmics offers online GO and KEGG enrichment analysis tools to facilitate further data exploration. In summary, iCellOmics provides a valuable starting point for investigating gene-phenotype relationships in industrially relevant cell lines and supports cell-line engineering and the development of improved producer lines.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: ThermoMutDB 2.0: semiautomated literature curation and structural enrichment of thermostability data for protein mutations.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Experimental measurements of protein thermodynamic stability are essential for understanding the relationship between protein structure and function, the molecular consequences of mutations, and their potential implications for protein malfunction and disease. However, extracting these data from the literature remains constrained by labor-intensive manual curation. Here, we present ThermoMutDB 2.0, a scalable framework for semiautomated literature curation and systematic structural enrichment. It introduces a major architectural redesign that integrates a large language model with rule-based entity recognition to identify and prioritize publications reporting experimentally measured effects of protein mutations on thermostability, while retaining expert validation as the final curation step. Complementing this literature-processing workflow, ThermoMutDB 2.0 systematically enriches curated mutations with mutant structural models, enabling interactive three-dimensional contextualization of experimentally derived thermodynamic data. Applied to the literature retrieved from January 1976 to the most recent search update in 2026, the pipeline screened 5,934 candidate publications and prioritized 254 for expert review, resulting in the incorporation of 102 articles and 1763 new entries. Rather than representing a simple expansion of database content, ThermoMutDB 2.0 establishes an extensible human-in-the-loop architecture in which automated literature triage, expert curation, and structural modeling operate as an integrated workflow. This redesign provides a sustainable foundation for continuous database maintenance and for linking experimental protein stability measurements with their structural context (available at http://thermomutdb.pathotrack.health/).

Nucleic Acids Research.title: PlantPAN 5.0: updated database for integrating multiomics evidence and exploring multilayered transcriptional regulatory networks in plants.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Plant Promoter Analysis Navigator (PlantPAN) 5.0 (https://plantpan.itps.ncku.edu.tw/) is an integrated multiomics resource for investigating plant cis-regulatory elements and transcriptional regulatory networks. This release expands genome annotations and promoter sequences to 240 species and provides 71 040 transcription factor (TF) annotations and 7762 nonredundant binding matrices. Its companion database, PCBase 3.0, substantially expands ChIP-seq data and newly incorporates ATAC-seq, bisulfite-sequencing, and four Hi-C-based chromatin interaction datasets for Arabidopsis thaliana. The new Differential Analysis function enables comparison of TF binding, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation across conditions. The redesigned Promoter Analysis interface provides TF family-level statistics, with a Pattern Overview panel integrating TF-binding site (TFBS) densities, plant DNA large language model-predicted open-chromatin regions, CpG-rich regions, and tandem repeats. Two new modules are introduced: (i) Transcriptome Regulatory Analysis and Coexpression, where candidate regulatory TFs and shared cis-elements in gene sets are prioritized through differential expression and coexpression analysis, and (ii) Interaction Topology Analysis for Chromatin and TFs, where chromatin interaction regions are integrated to reveal potentially coregulated genes and their shared TFs and predicted TFBSs. A Dockerized package enables large-scale local promoter analyses, with data privacy. Therefore, PlantPAN 5.0 is a comprehensive framework for discovering plant transcriptional regulatory mechanisms.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Gene Expression Nebulas 2.0: an updated resource of gene expression profiles by incorporating more datasets, annotations, and functionalities.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Gene Expression Nebulas (GEN; https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gen/) is an open-access database that provides standardized transcriptomic profiles and manually curated metadata across diverse species. Compared with the previous release, the updated GEN has expanded in terms of datasets from 323 to 668, samples from 50 500 to 102 679, cells from 15 540 169 to 23 461 252, and species from 30 to 100. GEN 2.0 adds spatial transcriptomics data and disease-associated expression annotations from 82 human bulk RNA-seq datasets spanning 62 disease categories, including distinct subtypes, across 12 disease systems. In addition, it has been significantly upgraded by providing high-quality gene expression profiles for artificial intelligence applications, a web-based service to accept transcriptomic data submission, and an updated online analysis tool for gene expression comparisons across species, tissues, and diseases. Together, GEN offers more comprehensive, standardized gene expression profiles across diverse species and thus serves as a fundamental resource for uncovering molecular functional mechanisms and deciphering complex regulatory architecture.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: IsoAPA: a multi-species long-read RNA-seq atlas of isoform-resolved alternative polyadenylation.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Genes are often treated as the primary unit of regulation, yet it is transcript isoforms that ultimately execute regulatory output, shaping mRNA stability, localization, and protein production. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) diversifies these outcomes by generating alternative 3' ends. However, existing resources catalogue polyadenylation sites (PASs) primarily as genomic events, obscuring the transcript isoforms on which individual sites are used. Here, we present IsoAPA (https://isoapa.sls.cuhk.edu.hk), a systematically curated database that leverages PacBio and Oxford Nanopore long-read RNA-seq to resolve PASs while preserving their native isoform context. The current release contains over 2.3 million transcript-resolved PAS records from 816 sample groups across 99 species. IsoAPA reveals widespread PAS multiplicity within fixed transcript backbones, with a mean of 2.52 distinct retained PASs per observed transcript in the union across 286 human sample groups. Transcript-level analysis further uncovers PAS usage patterns that are masked by gene-level aggregation, both in PAS diversity and in context-dependent dominant-site usage. By anchoring each terminal site within its assigned transcript model, IsoAPA reframes APA analysis from a gene-centred description of terminal-site usage to an isoform-resolved view of transcript-end regulation.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: scGWAS-DB: an integrated database bridging GWAS to tissue-resolved single-cell contexts.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The integration of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) with single-cell RNA sequencing has enabled the dissection of complex trait architectures across tissue-resolved cellular contexts. However, existing resources lack the ability to identify hub genes underlying trait-cell-type associations, dissect gene-gene interaction topologies, or detect shared genes across multiple traits. Here, we present single-cell-assisted Genome-Wide Association Study DataBase (scGWAS-DB) (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/scgwasdb), an integrated database that bridges population-scale genetics with single-cell biology. scGWAS-DB integrates 3,649 high-quality GWAS datasets with single-cell atlases spanning 74 human tissues and 1,713 cell types. From these data, we identified 213,992 significant triplets, encompassing 821,480 gene-gene interactions. Among them, we further distinguished 584,944 co-occurrent and 7,365 mutual exclusive gene-gene interaction patterns. Systematic integration of these networks revealed recurrent cellular signatures across diverse diseases. Collectively, scGWAS-DB provides a systematic resource for interpreting the cellular basis of complex traits, prioritizing hub genes and cell types that could provide insights in future studies of drug target development and disease-relevant cellular circuit discovery.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: gcPathogen 2.0: an expanded multi-omics database advancing global pathogen surveillance and One Health research.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Launched in 2024, gcPathogen established a critical foundation for the genomic surveillance of human pathogens. Here, we present gcPathogen 2.0, a major multi-omics update designed to address key analytical bottlenecks, including the integration of genomic and transcriptional profiles, systematic tracking of cross-habitat distribution, and large-scale discovery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). This release expands coverage from 1134 to 1506 pathogenic species, spanning 557 bacteria, 508 fungi, 258 viruses, and 183 parasites, and increases total genomic records past 2.3 million. By incorporating 12 597 transcriptomes across 148 species, gcPathogen 2.0 bridges the gap between gene carriage and functional expression for risk assessment. Furthermore, the platform integrates 285 925 pathogen metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) spanning human, animal, and environmental niches. Mapped across 68 Environment Ontology (ENVO) habitat categories, these MAGs enable comprehensive tracking of cross-habitat distribution of pathogens, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), virulence factors (VFs), and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Leveraging a nonredundant reference set curated from seven public databases, we identified over 77 million AMPs belonging to >55 000 families across 438 bacterial pathogens. Finally, pan-genome analyses of 440 bacterial species map intraspecies functional distributions across core, accessory, and unique gene repertoires. gcPathogen 2.0 is publicly accessible at https://nmdc.cn/gcpathogen/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: The Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) in 2026: updates of immune receptor data.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Immune Epitope Database (IEDB, iedb.org) is a freely available resource cataloging experimentally defined immune epitopes and, where reported, the immune receptors that recognize them. The IEDB currently records ∼235 000 distinct T cell receptors and ∼6400 distinct B cell receptors/antibodies with experimentally verified epitope specificity. Here, we describe recent updates to the IEDB, centered on a comprehensive revision of these receptor data. Because receptors were curated from 3879 references spanning decades, heterogeneity in gene nomenclature and CDR delimitation presents challenges for computational analyses and user queries. We rebuilt the standardization and validation pipeline to compute IUIS/IMGT-compliant V/D/J gene names and consistently delimited V domain, CDR1, 2, 3, and Junction sequences, and identify anomalous receptors from 822 references for re-curation. The IEDB web interface was expanded to include receptor search features directly on the homepage, support V/J gene and species options in the refined receptor search, and direct data export in the Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire (AIRR) format. We anticipate that the improved data quality will simplify bioinformatics analyses and facilitate integration into cross-repository data resources, such as the AIRR Knowledge Commons.

Nature Genetics.abstract: Nature Genetics, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02830-5This study presents jaxQTL, an efficient count-based pseudobulk single-cell eQTL mapping framework. When applied to OneK1K data, jaxQTL discovers more eGenes than existing methods while running faster.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Elevated ozone reshapes wheat root-associated microbiomes through coordinated plant responses and rhizosphere environmental filtering.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Elevated tropospheric ozone (O3) threatens crop productivity, but how O3-induced changes in plant responses influence root-associated microbiomes remains unclear. We investigated the responses of microbial communities inhabiting the rhizosphere and root endosphere to elevated O3 using four cultivars grown under ambient and 1.5-fold ambient O3 in a field-based free-air O3-concentration enrichment (FACE) system. Plant traits, root-released organic carbon (ROC), rhizosphere properties, extracellular enzyme activities, and bacterial and fungal communities were jointly analyzed. Elevated O3 reduced yield and root biomass, with cultivar-dependent changes in ROC. Elevated O3 consistently increased rhizosphere pH and altered microbial resource allocation, increasing ecoenzymatic vector length by 4.1% and decreasing vector angle by 4.6%. Bacterial communities showed a stronger response than fungal taxonomic communities, particularly in the rhizosphere. However, variation partitioning indicated that soil properties, especially pH, rather than O3 treatment alone, provided the strongest independent explanation for bacterial community variation. Fungal communities showed limited taxonomic turnover but exhibited shifts in predicted trophic guilds, including increased pathotroph- and saprotroph-associated groups and decreased symbiotroph-containing guilds under elevated O3. These results demonstrate that elevated O3 reshapes the wheat root-associated microbiome through coordinated changes in plant performance, rhizosphere environmental filtering, and microbial functional strategies, highlighting the importance of plant-mediated processes in regulating belowground responses to atmospheric change.IMPORTANCEElevated tropospheric O3 is an increasing threat to crop production, but its effects on belowground microbial processes remain poorly understood. This study demonstrates that O3-induced root-associated microbiome changes are closely linked with altered plant carbon allocation and rhizosphere environmental conditions rather than O3 exposure also. By integrating plant traits, soil properties, extracellular enzyme allocation, and microbial community analyses, we reveal a compartment-specific plant-soil-microbiome response to elevated O3. These findings improve our understanding of how atmospheric pollution may reshape crop-associated microbial functions and soil ecological processes under future climate change.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: A conserved CusR-dependent regulatory pathway couples copper homeostasis with oxidative stress resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Host-derived copper toxicity is a central antimicrobial strategy that restricts bacterial survival during infection, yet how pathogens integrate copper detoxification with oxidative stress resistance remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify the response regulator CusR as a pivotal coordinator of copper homeostasis and oxidative stress defense in Klebsiella pneumoniae. Loss of cusR results in profound defects in copper tolerance, marked intracellular copper accumulation, and hypersensitivity to hydrogen peroxide, accompanied by elevated intracellular reactive oxygen species. Mechanistically, CusR directly activates the cusCFBA copper efflux operon through promoter binding, whereas regulation of the copA transporter occurs independently of CusR. Importantly, a conserved aspartate residue (D56) within CusR is essential for its activity; both plasmid-based and chromosomal substitution of this residue abolish copper efflux regulation, disrupt copper homeostasis, and exacerbate oxidative stress susceptibility. Comparative sequence analysis further demonstrates that this residue is highly conserved across diverse bacterial species, underscoring its evolutionary importance in copper-responsive signaling. Collectively, our findings reveal a conserved Asp-dependent CusR-CusCFBA regulatory axis that couples copper detoxification to oxidative stress resistance, enabling bacterial adaptation to host-imposed copper stress.IMPORTANCECopper intoxication is an important host-mediated antimicrobial strategy that challenges bacterial pathogens during infection. Although copper resistance systems have been extensively studied, how bacteria coordinate copper detoxification with protection against oxidative stress remains poorly understood. In this study, we identify the response regulator CusR as a key factor linking copper homeostasis and oxidative stress resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae. We demonstrate that CusR directly controls the cusCFBA copper efflux system through promoter binding and that a conserved aspartate residue is essential for this regulatory function. Loss of CusR disrupts copper balance, increases reactive oxygen species accumulation, and reduces bacterial resistance to oxidative stress. These findings reveal a conserved regulatory mechanism that integrates metal stress adaptation with oxidative stress defense, providing new insights into how bacterial pathogens survive under host-imposed environmental pressures.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Hybrid genome assemblies of Bacteroidota isolates uncover mobile genetic elements, antimicrobial resistance genes, and novel antimicrobial peptides.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Members of the phylum Bacteroidota dominate the mammalian gut microbiota and represent promising candidates for next-generation probiotics. However, the resolution of complete Bacteroidota genomes is often hindered by extensive repetitive sequences and mobile genetic elements, a technical challenge further exacerbated by high intraspecies diversity and strain-level variants that drive assembly fragmentation and preclude the recovery of contiguous scaffolds. We recently isolated 18 strains that belonged to the Bacteroidales order of Bacteroidota from mouse ceca, human feces, and tortoise stool, which we now sequenced using both Illumina and Oxford Nanopore platforms. We developed a specialized assembly workflow to reconstruct high-resolution genomes and characterize their extrachromosomal landscapes. The hybrid pipeline yielded 2 fully closed, single-contig chromosomes, 10 almost closed genomes, and 6 draft assemblies. Genomic integrity was exceptionally high, with completeness scores ranging from 99.6% to 100% and contamination levels below 2%. A total of 12 circular plasmids were detected across 10 isolates; eight isolates harbored a single plasmid, while two isolates (241163E and 241171E) each carried two distinct circular plasmids. Seven of these plasmids were experimentally confirmed through isolation and sequencing, and five were classified as viral contigs. Functional annotation revealed a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial resistance genes and identified several predicted antimicrobial peptides in the assemblies through machine-learning analysis, of which two selected ones were experimentally verified. Overall, the resulting assemblies provide a reliable foundation for tracking mobile genetic elements, assessing resistance potential, and mining bioactive peptides in Bacteroidota species intended for therapeutic development. [IMPORTANCE] Bacteria in the phylum Bacteroidota are essential to mammalian gut health and are currently being developed as advanced probiotics. However, their complex DNA often prevents scientists from mapping their complete genetic blueprints, which can leave hidden traits like antibiotic resistance undetected. In this study, we combined two advanced DNA sequencing methods to create highly accurate and complete genetic maps for 18 Bacteroidota isolates from humans, mice, and tortoise. We successfully uncovered small, elusive DNA rings (potential plasmids) and confirmed their physical presence in the laboratory. Furthermore, we identified genes responsible for antibiotic resistance and used artificial intelligence to discover new antimicrobial peptides. This research provides a crucial foundation for the scientific community to accurately track mobile genes, rigorously evaluate the safety of potential gut therapeutics, and discover novel molecules for medical applications.

mBio.title: Bacterial extracellular vesicles as carriers of genetic and regulatory messages.
mBio.abstract: Although bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are increasingly recognized as mediators of communication, the contribution of their nucleic acid cargo remains poorly understood. Providing an overview of BEV-nucleic acid content and their roles, this review first examines their true significance. In particular, it highlights why they should not be treated as bulk cargo, given that DNA and RNA contents exhibit various sub-vesicular localizations that may define their ecological roles. We propose that this heterogeneity allows viewing BEVs as distinct subpopulations. Furthermore, recent studies increasingly propose the involvement of DNA associated with BEVs in horizontal gene transfer between bacteria and that of vesicular small RNA (sRNA) during host-bacteria interactions. Overall, this review offers insights into considering BEVs in an ecological context based on notable recent studies.

mBio.title: Intraspecies competition reveals branched-chain amino acid homeostasis as a targetable metabolic vulnerability in uropathogenic E. coli.
mBio.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most prevalent bacterial infections worldwide, with ~50% of women experiencing at least one UTI in their lifetime. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) is the causative agent of ~80% of UTIs. In contrast, asymptomatic bacteriuria E. coli 83972 (ABU 83972) colonizes the human urinary bladder without causing symptoms and inflammation. Deliberate colonization with ABU 83972 reduced UTI incidence in patients with voiding disorders. However, the mechanisms by which ABU 83972 outcompetes uropathogens in the urinary tract remain poorly understood and are the focus of this report. We performed comparative metabolomics to identify metabolites that promoted the fitness of ABU 83972 in human urine compared to UPEC strain CFT073. Competition assays were conducted between ABU 83972 and UPEC CFT073 in human urine supplemented with select metabolites that were differentially abundant in metabolome profiling. There was a significant reduction in the fitness of ABU 83972 when supplemented with branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) such as leucine and isoleucine in a dose-dependent manner. Further, we identified that BrnQ, a low-affinity BCAA importer, is the main determinant of fitness advantage of ABU 83972 over UPEC. Using isogenic mutants, genetic complementation, amino acid analysis, cell culture, chemical inhibition of BCAA biosynthesis, and mouse models of UTI, we demonstrate that BCAA homeostasis represents a unique nutritional vulnerability in UPEC that could be targeted with chemical inhibitors. In summary, our study highlights that intraspecies competition between commensal and pathogenic strains could be used to detect novel fitness mechanisms and metabolic bottlenecks. [IMPORTANCE] Millions of people suffer from urinary tract infection (UTI) globally, and uropathogenic E. coli is the main cause of UTI. A urinary probiotic strain of E. coli has been used clinically to prevent UTI in some high-risk groups for recurrent UTI for more than 25 years. However, the mechanism of competition between the probiotic and pathogenic strains is not clear. We demonstrate that competition for specific amino acids is critical for the probiotic to compete against the pathogen. Our study identifies specific amino acid import and biosynthetic processes as targets for controlling UPEC growth during UTI.

mBio.title: A convergent proline biosynthetic step couples cell wall integrity to virulence in Cryptococcus neoformans.
mBio.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Metabolic adaptation is essential for the pathogenicity of the opportunistic fungus Cryptococcus neoformans. Although amino acid biosynthesis pathways are critical fitness determinants in fungal pathogens, the physiological contributions of proline biosynthesis remain incompletely understood, with most studies focusing on proline catabolism. Here, we characterized the proline biosynthetic enzymes Pro1, Pro2, and Pro3 in C. neoformans. Proline is produced by two routes that converge on Δ1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C): a de novo pathway from glutamate via Pro1 and Pro2, and an arginine-derived bypass via Car1 and Car2-both requiring Pro3 for the final reduction of P5C to proline. Although all biosynthetic mutants were strictly auxotrophic for proline, their requirements for virulence differed markedly: in a murine infection model, pro1Δ and pro2Δ mutants retained full virulence, whereas pro3Δ exhibited significantly attenuated virulence accompanied by growth defects and impaired cell wall integrity. Genetic disruption of P5C-generating routes partially restored distinct pro3Δ phenotypes, with PRO2 deletion alleviating delayed growth, and combined PRO2 and CAR2 deletion partially restoring cell size, while cell wall defects remained unresolved. This dissociation indicates that growth requires proper balance of P5C-generating metabolic flux, whereas cell wall integrity depends on a distinct mechanism that is not resolved by blocking P5C production. Together, these findings identify Pro3 as a metabolic gatekeeper coupling proline biosynthesis to cell wall homeostasis, establishing the biosynthetic branch of proline metabolism as a previously unappreciated determinant of fungal pathobiology. [IMPORTANCE] Cryptococcus neoformans is a leading cause of fungal meningitis worldwide, causing life-threatening infections primarily in immunocompromised individuals. To survive within the human host, this pathogen must synthesize essential nutrients through de novo biosynthesis when host-derived supplies are limited. Although proline catabolism has been studied extensively in fungal pathogens, the physiological roles of individual proline biosynthetic enzymes in human fungal pathogens remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that the terminal enzyme Pro3, but not the upstream enzymes Pro1 and Pro2, is selectively required for full virulence in a murine model. Pro3 supports pathobiological fitness by promoting growth under host-relevant conditions and maintaining cell wall integrity. These findings highlight the importance of proline biosynthesis beyond nutrient production and link this pathway to growth, cell wall integrity, and virulence in C. neoformans.

Coupled Geophysical and Technoeconomic Industrial Growth Constraints on Geological Carbon Storage Scale-Up: Application to UK Offshore Resources.
Environmental Science & Technology.abstract: Geological carbon dioxide storage is central to meeting many national climate change commitments, but large-scale deployment may be limited by both techno-economic rates of growth and physics-based processes imposed by subsurface geology. We develop a modeling framework for the assessment of feasible CO2 storage scale-up trajectories that unifies constraints arising from industrial rates of growth, dynamic injection rate limits from reservoir pressurization, and static maximum cumulative storage resource. We employ logistic and Gompertz models to represent policy-compliant deployment trajectories, parametrized by the total cumulative storage resource. We then use a simplified physics model to estimate the resulting regional subsurface pressurization along these trajectories. Growth curves where reservoir pressurization exceeds safe limits are updated by reducing the static storage resource until residing in the safe deployment range. The result is both a growth trajectory and static storage resource achievable subject to injectivity limits. Applying the framework to the United Kingdom (UK), we find that offshore storage resources are sufficient to accommodate all government midcentury deployment rate scenarios up to 175 Mt yr-1. Cumulative storage of up to 78 Gt, representing a reference estimate of the UK storage resource base used in national planning, can be achieved under Gompertz growth trajectories. The more aggressive logistic trajectories are constrained by reservoir pressure, limiting the achievable resource base to 69 Gt. The framework is transferable to other regions to assess the feasibility of policy-driven CO2 storage pathways under coupled industrial growth and geophysical constraints, informing national decarbonization planning and global integrated assessment models.

Environmental Science & Technology.title: Fingerprints of Airborne Plastics in Urban PM2.5: Applications and Implications.
Environmental Science & Technology.abstract: To better identify emission sources of airborne plastics, we employed nine plastic-associated chemicals (PlsACs) in 240 daily PM2.5 samples collected in Singapore during 2018-2020. A unique PlsAC, tris(2,4-ditert-butylphenyl) phosphate (I168O), is most abundant, accounting for 90% of the total quantified PlsACs and identifying at least 40% more PM2.5 linked to respirable airborne PlsACs. A newly resolved source of plastic production, use, and burning (PlasticPub) accounts for the highest fraction (37%) of the quantified PlsACs among the seven apportioned PM2.5 sources. Nearly all di-iso-butyl phthalate (DIBP) and more than half of di-n-butyl phthalate (DNBP) are attributed to two factors of Background and Marine aerosols, indicating their potential worldwide transport. More than 90% of diethyl phthalate (DEP) is associated with transported peat forest (PF) burning smoke, demonstrating involvement of anthropogenic activities. Following PlasticPub, Traffic & road dust is the second predominant source responsible for >20% of the near-range PlsACs and featured with a DNBP/di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP) concentration ratio of 2.2. The DNBP/DEHP concentration ratio higher than 1 can indicate nonexhaust emissions from on-road traffic due to abrasion of tires, brakes, and road markings. The average enrichment ratio of quantified PlsACs within PM2.5 (ng PlsACs per μg PM2.5) for each resolved source provides a basis for assessing strategies to cocontrol airborne plastics and PM2.5.

Environmental Science & Technology.title: Modeling Decadal Organosulfates in Particulate Matter to Improve Estimations of Aerosol Hygroscopicity in the United States.
Environmental Science & Technology.abstract: Organosulfates (OSs) can comprise a substantial fraction of secondary organic aerosol and exhibit significantly different hygroscopicity than inorganic sulfates, yet their spatiotemporal prevalence and climatic impacts remain poorly constrained because speciated measurements are sparse and common chemical transport models do not explicitly represent OS formation. This study develops a flexible and robust modeling framework to quantify isoprene-derived OS (iOS) concentrations and OS impacts on aerosol hygroscopicity (κ) across the contiguous United States (U.S.) for summers spanning 2013-2022. Using the Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ) model with updated iOS chemistry, simulations reproduce Interagency Monitoring of Protected Visual Environments (IMPROVE) network-derived organosulfur and inorganic sulfate and agree with speciated iOS measurements from filter analyses. OS concentrations are elevated in the eastern U.S., with summertime mean values up to 0.51 μg m-3. OS formation produces a net 5.6% decrease in κ (direct OS contribution, +2.8%; indirect, -8.4% via sulfate reduction).
