Journal of Virology.title: APOBEC3 antagonism fully explains HIV-1 Vif essentiality in THP-1 cells under interferon and differentiation conditions.
Journal of Virology.abstract: HIV-1 virion infectivity factor (Vif) counteracts APOBEC3 (A3) proteins by targeting them for proteasomal degradation, thereby preventing lethal G-to-A mutations and loss of infectivity. However, Vif also degrades additional cellular proteins, raising the possibility that its essential role in infectious virion production may extend beyond A3 antagonism, particularly under inflammatory or differentiation conditions. Whether such conditions reveal additional essential Vif targets remains unresolved. Here, using interferon (IFN)-stimulated or phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA)-differentiated THP-1 monocytic cells, we directly addressed this question. Although type I IFN and PMA markedly suppressed viral production through Vif-independent mechanisms, ΔVif viruses produced from stimulated parental cells exhibited severely reduced infectivity. In contrast, disruption of A3A-A3G fully restored ΔVif infectivity to wild-type levels under all conditions tested. G-to-A mutations were attributable exclusively to A3 proteins under both IFN and PMA stimulation, whereas IFN-induced, A3-independent blocks to reverse transcription were not antagonized by Vif. Moreover, Vif-mediated degradation of the non-A3 targets PPP2R5 family proteins did not measurably contribute to virion infectivity under these conditions. Across diverse HIV-1 strains, the requirement for Vif in this experimental system was strictly dependent on A3 family proteins. These findings indicate that, under the conditions examined here, the essential role of Vif is fully explained by antagonism of A3-mediated restriction. Our results further suggest that counteracting A3-mediated restriction and mutagenesis represents a major evolutionary pressure shaping Vif.IMPORTANCEA3 proteins are potent intrinsic antiviral factors that restrict HIV-1 by inducing lethal mutations and impairing reverse transcription. The viral protein Vif counteracts A3-mediated restriction, yet it also targets additional host proteins, raising questions about whether its essential role extends beyond A3 antagonism under inflammatory conditions. Myeloid cells mount interferon (IFN) responses and undergo transcriptional reprogramming upon differentiation, environments in which additional Vif functions could emerge. Using an A3A-A3G-null monocytic cell model, we show that even under IFN stimulation or phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA)-induced differentiation, the requirement for Vif in maintaining HIV-1 infectivity is due to A3 proteins. In contrast, Vif does not counteract IFN-induced, A3-independent restriction pathways, highlighting functional specificity. These findings establish the A3-Vif axis as the central determinant of Vif dependency and suggest that counteracting A3-mediated restriction and mutagenesis represents a major evolutionary pressure shaping Vif. Targeting Vif may therefore expose HIV-1 to intrinsic inactivation, even in inflammatory environments.

Journal of Virology.title: BK virus-neutralizing antibodies converge on a shared site of vulnerability on VP1.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] BK virus is a human polyomavirus that infects approximately 80% of adults and establishes lifelong latency. Although primary infection is typically asymptomatic, viral reactivation in kidney transplant recipients can cause BK virus-associated nephropathy, leading to graft dysfunction and rejection. Despite the clinical severity of viral reactivation, antiviral treatment options remain limited. Notably, high serum titers of BK virus-neutralizing antibodies are associated with reduced BK virus DNAemia in kidney transplant recipients, suggesting an important role for humoral immunity in controlling viral replication. Here, we curated a comprehensive database of human antibodies targeting the major capsid protein VP1 by integrating previously reported sequences with newly generated data. Sequence analysis revealed only limited convergence among these antibodies. Nevertheless, functional and biochemical characterization showed that most neutralizing antibodies compete for overlapping epitopes, indicating convergence on a common antigenic site within the receptor-binding cleft of VP1. Together, these findings define an immunodominant site of vulnerability on the BK virus capsid and provide a mechanistic basis for the rational design of vaccines and antibody-based therapies. [IMPORTANCE] BK virus (BKV) reactivation is a common complication in kidney transplant recipients, yet no approved antivirals are currently available. The standard of care consists of reducing immunosuppressive therapy, which carries an inherent risk of graft rejection. Antibodies represent promising therapeutic agents for the prevention and treatment of viral infections, particularly when effective vaccines are unavailable. Elucidating the dominant mechanisms of antibody-mediated protection is crucial for guiding the design and optimization of antibody-based therapies. In this study, we identify novel potent neutralizing antibodies against BKV, compare them with previously reported monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), and demonstrate that they compete for binding. Our findings show that most neutralizing mAbs converge on the receptor-binding cleft of VP1, identifying this region as both a major site of vulnerability and a hotspot for immune-driven viral escape, with important implications for therapeutic design.

Journal of Virology.title: Pathogenic mechanisms of Echovirus 18-induced encephalitis in a novel hFcRn transgenic mouse model.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Echovirus 18 (E18) poses an escalating neurological threat in children, with its complex pathogenesis impeded by the absence of robust animal models for comprehensive mechanistic investigation. This study establishes an E18-induced viral encephalitis (VE) model in 7-day-old human neonatal Fc receptor (hFcRn) transgenic mice. After intracranial inoculation with 4.0  ×  106  PFU of E18, mice developed marked signs of infection, characterized by progressive weight loss, motor impairment, elevated viral loads in the brain, and histopathological evidence of VE, ultimately resulting in approximately 75% mortality. The E18-infected mouse brains were accompanied by lymphocytic and granulocytic infiltration, neuronal shrinkage, and focal hemorrhage, with magnetic resonance imaging revealing prominent signal abnormalities in the subarachnoid space and periventricular regions. Interestingly, although all cell types of the brain can serve as carriers of the virus at the single-cell level, E18 exhibits distinct cellular tropism by preferentially targeting astrocytes and microglia rather than neurons and neurofilaments. Additionally, E18 infection orchestrates a complex and adaptive immune response, with dynamic changes among astrocytic subtypes reflecting the evolution of this immune response. Overall, this study successfully establishes a disease model that enhances our understanding of E18-induced encephalitis and provides a valuable platform for evaluating therapeutic interventions and developing vaccines.IMPORTANCEE18 represents an important pathogen in infectious diseases, with potential neurological complications that warrant further investigation. However, due to ethical and technical limitations, its neuropathological mechanisms have long remained unexplored. This study presents a novel encephalitis model using 7-day-old hFcRnTg mice. The integration of MRI, histopathology, and multi-omics analysis elucidated the molecular mechanisms of viral neural invasion, offering critical insights into pediatric viral encephalitis and potential therapeutic strategies. This animal model provides a valuable platform for understanding E18-induced encephalitis mechanisms and evaluating potential therapeutics and vaccines.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Ecological and genomic insights into seaweed-associated Verrucomicrobiota from the Gulf of Mannar.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Members of the phylum Verrucomicrobiota are increasingly recognized for their ecological versatility and capacity to degrade complex polysaccharides across diverse marine and freshwater ecosystems. In this study, we recovered 11 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) affiliated with the orders Puniceicoccales and Verrucomicrobiales from seaweed-associated microbiomes in the Gulf of Mannar, India. Verrucomicrobiota constituted 0.6%-2.9% of the total bacterial community across the analyzed algal samples, indicating their consistent presence but low abundance in these habitats. Five high-quality MAGs (JB022, JB024, JB025, JB027, JB023; completeness >90%, contamination <5%) were selected for detailed genomic and ecological characterization. Phylogenomic analyses revealed that these MAGs form distinct lineages within known Verrucomicrobiota families, expanding the known diversity of this phylum in marine algal ecosystems. Comparative genomic analysis showed that these genomes encode diverse biosynthetic gene clusters and a rich repertoire of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) and sulfatases, suggesting adaptation to the degradation of polysaccharides typical of seaweed substrates. These binned genomes also possess genes related to fermentative metabolism, nitrogen fixation, and partial denitrification, indicating metabolic versatility and potential contributions to nutrient cycling within algal holobionts. These findings reveal that seaweed-associated Verrucomicrobiota from the Gulf of Mannar represent phylogenomically distinct and functionally specialized lineages with ecological relevance in carbon and nitrogen cycling in coastal marine ecosystems. This study provides the first genomic insights into seaweed-associated Verrucomicrobiota from India, representing potential new taxa and underscoring their potential roles in polysaccharide degradation and holobiont functioning. [IMPORTANCE] Coastal biomes harbor a rich diversity of microorganisms, and only a few studies have focused on the diversity and functional role of members of the phylum Verrucomicrobiota. Despite their low abundance, members of the phylum Verrucomicrobiota can play an important role in regulating the fate of carbon within marine ecosystems. This study presents the first identification of novel Verrucomicrobial taxa from India, particularly from the Gulf of Mannar, a marine biodiversity hotspot with limited prior microbial investigations. Through metagenome-resolved genomic analysis, this work infers the potential ecological role of these newly discovered Verrucomicrobiota members and suggests their probable role in the carbon cycling and ecosystem processes.
